newsitem.title: USA: GE union members to vote on contract.
newsitem.headline: GE union members to vote on contract.

text.p: General Electric Co said Thursday that members of two unions representing some 27,000 employees have reached a tentative agreement on a three-year contract calling for an 8.75 percent general pay rise.
GE said in a statement that general pay rates will rise by 3.75 percent in June 1997, 2.5 percent in June 1998, and 2.5 percent in June 1999.
Members of the unions will vote on the contracts next week.

GE said the tentative agreements were reached on June 29 by negotiators representing GE and the International Union of Electronic Workers (IUE) and the United Electrical Workers of America, following five weeks of bargaining.

The general pay increases, six cost-of-living adjustments and a wage structure increase for higher wage-rate employees are expected to raise the pay of the average employee by more than 13 percent over the contract period -- assuming 2.9 percent for annual inflation, GE said.
The contract mainly covers workers who build aircraft engines, locomotives, appliances and other products.
On the issue of job security, GE said the contract provides notice and local decision bargaining on sub-contracting and similar actions.
Jobs preserved through the decision bargaining process will be protected for two years or until the end of the contract, it said.
GE said it was informed by union officials on Wednesday that their negotiating committees and conference boards are recommending approval of the tentative agreements.
"We've done what we said we would do -- come home with a breakthrough contract," AFL-CIO Coordinated Bargaining Committee Chairman Ed Fire told a news conference.
"The billion-dollar contract is the richest in the history of collective bargaining at General Electric," Fire said.
"It's going to be ratified by a huge, huge margin... I'm projecting an 80 percent ratification (margin)," he said.
Fire said the contract was in some ways not ideal, but it included important provisions on job security.
